recall.question: What is the diffusion recipe?
recall.answer: Generative modeling by reversing a fixed noising process: the forward chain adds Gaussian noise, the learned reverse chain removes it one step at a time, starting from white noise.

recall.question: What does objective 3 ask the learner to do?
recall.answer: Reduce the ELBO to the noise-prediction objective.

keyTerms.definition: The fixed Markov chain x_0, ..., x_T adding Gaussian noise.
The per-step noise levels in (0, 1), small in practice.
alpha_1 * ... * alpha_t: the accumulated shrinkage.
The noisy state at any time step in closed form.

recall.question: What is the destroy-then-undestroy idea?
recall.answer: The forward chain turns any image into white noise through hundreds of tiny Gaussian steps. Learning becomes: given a noisy sample at time t, recover the added noise. That is noise removal, not generation, a supervised task.

recall.question: What is the closed form of x_t given x_0?
recall.answer: x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) epsilon-hat_t, epsilon-hat_t ~ N(0, I).

recall.question: Why must beta_t be small?
recall.answer: If beta_t is too large early, one step wipes out structure and the reverse model must make huge jumps the Gaussian reverse kernel cannot represent.

sections.title: SL-02: Reverse parameterization and the true posterior

keyTerms.definition: p_theta(x_{t-1} | x_t): the learned denoising steps.
q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0): Gaussian by the conditional-Gaussian formula.
The weighted average of x_0 and x_t.
(1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) / (1 - alpha-bar_t) * beta_t.

recall.question: Why is the true reverse posterior Gaussian?
recall.answer: Conditioning on x_0 as well as x_t, the true reverse kernel is tractable: x_1..x_T are jointly Gaussian given x_0, so q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) is Gaussian by the conditional-Gaussian formula.

recall.question: What does training have to match?
recall.answer: One mean vector: with sigma_t^2 = beta-tilde_t the KL is half the squared Mahalanobis distance of the means. Nothing else is learned.

recall.question: In the computed example, what is mu-tilde_50?

sections.title: SL-03: ELBO to the denoising objective

keyTerms.definition: The lower bound on log p_theta(x_0) with the path as latent.
Reducing each ELBO term to a noise error.
epsilon_theta(x_t, t): the network predicting the added noise.
||epsilon - epsilon_theta(x_t, t)||^2 without the ELBO weights.

recall.question: What is the denoising reduction?
recall.answer: Reconstructing mu-tilde_t is equivalent to reconstructing the noise epsilon-hat_t. Each ELBO term becomes a weighted noise error; in practice the weights are dropped for the unweighted loss.

recall.question: What are the five training steps?
recall.answer: Sample x_0; sample t uniformly; sample noise epsilon; form x_t; take a gradient step on the loss. One sample, one step, one noise vector per update.

recall.question: Why not train with the exact ELBO weights?
recall.answer: They put heavy weight on small t. Ho et al. found this hurts sample quality: correct for likelihood, wrong for perceptual quality.

sections.title: SL-04: Sampling, continuous time, and the score

keyTerms.definition: Starting from x_T ~ N(0, I) and iterating t = T down to 1.
grad_x log p_t: the direction of increasing marginal density.
The continuous-time reverse process from Anderson's theorem.

recall.question: What is the score relation?
recall.answer: The score is the negative noise, rescaled: grad_x log q(x_t | x_0) = -epsilon-hat_t / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t). Predicting epsilon and predicting the score are the same task up to a known scalar.

recall.question: In the computed example, do the score and rescaled noise match?
recall.answer: Score -1.7829; rescaled noise -0.8417/0.4720 = -1.7829. They match.

recall.question: Why must the final sampling step have xi = 0?
recall.answer: Extra noise at t = 1 blurs the output.

keyTerms.definition: Assumed exactly spherical Gaussian after the forward chain.
The weighted ELBO on unseen data: a comparable number across models.

recall.question: What are the load-bearing assumptions?
recall.answer: q(x_T) exactly N(0,I); beta_t small; sigma_t^2 = beta-tilde_t fixed; images continuous while pixels are discrete; the unweighted loss is not the ELBO.

recall.question: How do you evaluate on held-out data?
recall.answer: Evaluate the ELBO with the exact weights (not the unweighted training loss) on held-out data. A tighter bound means a better density model; it is a bound, not the likelihood.

recall.question: Why can't ELBOs be compared across protocols?
recall.answer: Different discretization or different T makes the numbers meaningless. Fix the evaluation protocol first.

keyTerms.definition: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(x_t, sqrt(1 - beta_t) x_{t-1}, beta_t I).
x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) epsilon.
p_theta(x_{t-1} | x_t) = N(x_{t-1}, mu_theta(x_t, t), sigma_t^2 I).
L_t(theta) = ||epsilon - epsilon_theta(x_t, t)||^2.

recall.answer: Team A trains with the exact ELBO weights. Team B trains with the unweighted loss. Which wins on likelihood, which on sample quality, and why?
